name: Phase Three: Set Up Governance
title: Phase Three: Set Up Governance
answer: Phase Three of a pilot means completing governance before any student touches the tool: the tool is placed on the approved list with its limits recorded, a data privacy agreement is signed when student information is involved, a named owner is accountable for results, and families receive a short plain notice. It matters because skipping these steps creates problems later, when no one can answer a parent's question about data or when a vendor refuses to sign the agreement needed to scale.

sections.body: This idea is the governance groundwork that must be finished before a pilot begins, not after it is underway. It covers four concrete steps: listing the tool as approved with its limits noted, signing a data privacy agreement if student information is involved, naming an owner who reports results, and sending families a brief notice about what the tool does and whom to contact. The problem it solves is the corner cutting that happens when a teacher is enthusiastic and the school year is short. That shortcut looks harmless at the start but surfaces later, either when a parent asks what data was collected and nobody knows, or when a successful pilot cannot scale because the vendor will not sign the required agreement. A week of governance up front, the text argues, prevents months of cleanup.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, this phase runs before the first student login. The tool is added to the approved list with its limits written down, a data privacy agreement is signed where student information is involved, and one person is named as the pilot owner who reports results. Families of students in the pilot get a short, plain notice explaining the tool and giving a contact for questions. The text also places parent education here, through a short evening session or a one page guide covering how the school uses AI, what the pilot will test, and how families can help at home. The text does not give grade band variations for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or formal evidence label for this idea. Its support is practical and observational: the claim that many pilots cut corners here, usually because a teacher is excited and the school year is short, and that the cost appears later when a parent asks about collected data and nobody knows, or when a district tries to scale and finds the vendor will not sign the needed agreement. The text's own summary judgment is that a week spent on governance up front saves months of cleanup afterward. On that basis, this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are set out as consequences of skipping the phase: unanswered parent questions about data, and a pilot that cannot scale because the vendor will not sign the agreement it needs. The decisions that stay with people are naming the pilot owner who reports results, completing the approved list entry with its limits noted, signing the data privacy agreement when student information is involved, and issuing the family notice with a contact for questions. The text also treats family communication as a trust building step, noting that families who understand a pilot's purpose tend to support it even with concerns, while families who hear about it from their child tend to worry. Nothing here is legal advice; it describes practice.
